paras: The assault on Roland Alston at the Columbian Institution for the Deaf and Dumb occurred about noon on October 19, 1903, in Washington, D.C., when about fifty students "rushed" Alston, a young Black assistant janitor. They grabbed him and threw him down, and the pursuit ended only after he picked up a kitchen knife; he then left his job. The Evening Star covered it after rumors spread that the students had meant to lynch him.

Alston, who lived at 1645 Gales street northeast, worked as assistant janitor on the fourth floor of the college. By his account, students habitually threw waste paper and trash on the corridor floor. He then pinned up a note asking the men to stop, and someone else added lines using the words "hogs" and "dogs," for which Alston said he was not responsible.

Alston said a bell summoned him to where the students had assembled. "The men came at me in a rush," he told a Star reporter, adding that they grabbed him, tore his shirt and threw him down before he got away. According to the Star, the students gave up the pursuit only after Alston picked up a knife in the kitchen to defend himself.
Badly frightened, Alston left as soon as he received the money due him. No report of action by the school, the police or any court appears in the coverage.

The Evening Star ran the story on its eighth page on October 21 under the headline "'RUSHED' BY STUDENTS" and the deck "Young Colored Man at the Mercy of Gallaudet Boys." It cast the attack as a "college rush," gave most of its space to Alston's own account, and noted that he said the men had no reason to treat him as they did. The paper reported the rope-and-lynching rumor but described the reports as mostly exaggerated, and Alston said he saw no rope though he thought the students "meant business."

reader.title: Assault on Roland Alston at the Columbian Institution for the Deaf and Dumb
bases: About fifty students rushed, grabbed, threw down and pursued a Black janitor, who was not killed; lynching talk appears only as a rumor the paper called exaggerated (A1).
Only the Evening Star carried the story, largely in Alston's own words (A1); no other white or Black report was found.

accounts.label: Alston's account to the Star
accounts.gist: Students who littered his floor were angered by his note, to which someone else had added 'hogs' and 'dogs'; summoned by a bell, he was rushed, grabbed, had his shirt torn and was thrown down before getting away. He saw no rope but thought the students 'meant business.'

accounts.label: Current reports / rumor
accounts.gist: Reports circulating since Monday, which the Star called mostly exaggerated, held that the students had a rope and meant to lynch him.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined '"RUSHED" BY STUDENTS' and 'at the Mercy of Gallaudet Boys,' framed it as a 'college rush,' gave Alston's account at length and discounted the lynching rumor as exaggerated.
